mechanism.law: In a Lewis symbol, each dot around the element symbol represents one valence electron; the dot count is then used to determine the common or group valence.
mechanism.causal_direction: Count the dots in the Lewis symbol first, then use that valence-electron count to infer the element's usual bonding capacity.
boundary_conditions: Lewis symbols represent only the outer-shell electrons, not protected inner-shell electrons.
For main-group elements, the common valence is generally related either to the number of dots or to the number needed to complete eight.
An ion's Lewis symbol must reflect electron loss or gain relative to the neutral atom.

Cl⁻ has 7 valence electrons, the same as a neutral chlorine atom.
Na⁺ has 2 dots — sodium gained one electron, which is why it is positive.
Aluminium's common valence is 5 (8 − 3).
Oxygen has 8 valence electrons, because the octet rule says the outer shell has 8.

decision_hinge: Decide whether an ionic bond forms by electron transfer followed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

mechanism.law: An ionic or electrovalent bond forms when electron transfer produces positive and negative ions, and the oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction.

A nonmetal such as chlorine or fluorine can form an anion by gaining electron(s).
The electrovalence equals the number of unit charges on the ion.
The final formula must balance the total positive and negative charges.

decision_hinge: Decide the covalent bond order from the number of shared electron pairs between two atoms.

mechanism.law: A covalent bond is formed by sharing an electron pair; one shared pair gives a single bond, two shared pairs give a double bond, and three shared pairs give a triple bond.

boundary_conditions: Each combining atom contributes at least one electron to a shared pair in the Lewis-Langmuir description.

Multiple bonds are required when a single shared pair does not satisfy the octet condition for the bonded atoms.

Classify one shared pair as single and two shared pairs as double.

decision_hinge: Use resonance when no single Lewis structure can represent the observed bonding in a molecule or ion.

mechanism.law: When one Lewis structure cannot account for the observed bond parameters, multiple canonical structures with the same skeletal arrangement are used; the real species is the resonance hybrid, which is more stable and averages bond characteristics.
mechanism.causal_direction: Compare the predicted single and double bonds in a Lewis structure with observed equal or intermediate bond lengths, then represent the species by resonance forms and a hybrid.
boundary_conditions: Canonical forms do not have real independent existence.
The molecule does not switch between canonical forms for fractions of time.
Canonical forms must describe the same molecule or ion with the same skeletal arrangement.
Resonance stabilizes the molecule because the hybrid has lower energy than any single canonical form.

mx.cwo: The actual structure of CO3^2- is its most stable canonical form.
The O3 molecule keeps flipping between its two resonance structures, spending half its time in each.
The resonance hybrid is higher in energy than the individual canonical structures, so resonance destabilizes the molecule.
CH4 shows resonance because all four of its C-H bonds are equivalent.
The three C-O bonds in CO3^2- are equal because carbon is sp2 hybridized.
CH3COOH has another resonance form with the H atom moved onto the other oxygen.

decision_hinge: Apply Fajans' rules to judge the covalent character in an ionic bond.

mechanism.law: The covalent character of an ionic bond increases when a cation polarizes an anion, especially for a smaller or more highly charged cation and a larger anion.
mechanism.causal_direction: Evaluate cation size, cation charge, and anion size to infer how strongly the cation pulls anion electron density into the internuclear region.
boundary_conditions: A smaller cation has greater polarizing power than a larger cation of similar charge.
A higher cation charge increases covalent character.
A larger anion is more easily polarized than a smaller anion.
The rule refines the ideal ionic picture because real ionic bonds can have partial covalent character.

steps.step: Recognize that ionic bonds can have partial covalent character rather than being only ideal ionic.
Compare cation polarizing power: smaller size and greater charge increase covalent character.
Compare anion polarizability: a larger anion is more easily polarized and raises covalent character.
Infer greater covalent character where cation pull shifts more anion charge into the internuclear region.

mx.cwo: NaF, NaCl, NaBr and NaI have equal covalent character because the cation (Na+) is the same.
KCl has more covalent character than LiCl because the larger K+ ion polarizes the chloride ion more.
CO2 has more covalent character than SiO2 because C4+ is smaller and polarizes O2− more strongly than Si4+.
MgO is less covalent than NaCl because MgO has a much higher melting point, so it is more strongly ionic.

decision_hinge: Explain covalent bond formation in valence bond theory as an energy-minimum result of orbital overlap and competing forces.

mechanism.law: In valence bond theory, a stable covalent molecule forms when attractive interactions between nuclei and electrons outweigh repulsions as atoms approach, lowering potential energy to a minimum at the bond length.
mechanism.causal_direction: As two atoms approach, compare new attractions and repulsions; if attractions dominate until an equilibrium separation is reached, a stable bond forms and energy is released.
boundary_conditions: At very large separation, the atoms do not interact appreciably.
Electron-electron and nucleus-nucleus repulsions oppose bond formation.
For H2, the energy minimum corresponds to a stable molecule with bond length about 74 pm.
The released energy is associated with bond enthalpy, and energy must be supplied to dissociate the bond.

As H atoms approach, 1s overlap begins and new nucleus-electron attractions and electron/nucleus repulsions operate.

decision_hinge: Classify a covalent bond as sigma or pi from the direction and extent of atomic-orbital overlap.

mechanism.law: A sigma bond forms by end-to-end overlap along the internuclear axis, while a pi bond forms by sidewise overlap of parallel orbitals perpendicular to the internuclear axis; sigma overlap is larger and gives a stronger bond.
mechanism.causal_direction: Inspect the orbital orientation relative to the internuclear axis, then classify the overlap as axial for sigma or sidewise for pi.
boundary_conditions: Sigma overlap can arise from s-s, s-p, or p-p head-on overlap along the internuclear axis.
Pi overlap requires parallel orbital axes that remain perpendicular to the internuclear axis.
Positive, negative, or zero overlap depends on orbital phase and orientation.
Bond strength depends on extent of overlap; larger sigma overlap makes sigma bonds stronger than pi bonds.

Sidewise overlap of parallel p orbitals gives a sigma bond; head-on overlap along the internuclear axis gives the pi bond.
The Na-Cl bond is a sigma bond because the two ions lie on the line joining their centres.
The C=C double bond is a pi bond (both lines are pi bonds).
The C-H bond in ethene is a pi bond because the carbon is sp2 hybridised.

decision_hinge: Explain molecular-orbital formation as linear combination of atomic orbitals into bonding and antibonding orbitals.

decision_hinge: Recognize how Raoult's law and Henry's law are the same proportionality with different constants.

boundary_conditions: Use Raoult's form for volatile components of liquid solutions.
Use Henry's form for gases dissolved in liquids.
Keep temperature fixed when comparing the constants.

decision_hinge: Identify azeotropes and connect large Raoult's-law deviations to constant-boiling mixtures.

boundary_conditions: Use this only for binary mixtures that have the same liquid and vapour composition.
